description:
Our team built Ember Atlas for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots”. NASA’s two active-fire records see fire differently, so their counts can’t simply be put side by side. We turned them into one trustworthy record for Türkiye.

We merge MODIS and VIIRS detections into unique fire events, keep only vegetation fires, and calibrate the two sensors onto a single scale. On top of that we built a burning calendar and a recurrence-based alert system.
summary:
Ember Atlas is a web app that harmonizes NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP) into one burning-activity calendar for any area a user selects. It is built on real detections for Türkiye, 2018–2020 and 2024–2025. The sensors disagree: VIIRS reports about seven times as many vegetation-fire detections as Aqua, and in 2019 the two put the peak month two months apart. Ember Atlas puts VIIRS on the Aqua scale using a transparent, versioned calibration, with bootstrap uncertainty and held-out temporal and spatial tests, and removes static and offshore sources (28% of VIIRS detections).

On top of the calendar, an alert page gives emergency responders, firefighters, land managers and scientists role-specific alerts (Normal to Critical) for unusual weeks, plus a map of places where fire has recurred and how likely it is to recur, backtested on later years. It is a research estimate: no valid-observation coverage was available, and it uses no weather or fuel data. We label that openly. Consistent fire records help agencies anticipate critical periods and focus monitoring.
details:
Ember Atlas is an interactive satellite-based wildfire monitoring and data harmonization platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It addresses the challenge of combining active fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments into a consistent framework, making their data easier to compare, interpret, and analyze.

How does it work?

The platform processes active fire hotspot datasets obtained from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). It harmonizes observations from MODIS and VIIRS, accounting for differences in their spatial characteristics, detection frequencies, and observation patterns. Users can explore fire activity through interactive maps, temporal charts, analytical dashboards, and satellite comparison views. The platform also includes an alert interface that categorizes observed activity into different levels to help users interpret changes in fire detections.

We use Türkiye as our pilot region, with historical and recent satellite observations supporting the analysis. The system is designed to distinguish between a lack of detected hotspots and a lack of observation coverage, avoiding the misleading assumption that no detection always means no fire.

Benefits and intended impact

Ember Atlas aims to:

  • Improve the comparability of MODIS and VIIRS fire observations.
  • Provide a clearer picture of wildfire activity across time and geographic areas.
  • Help researchers identify differences between satellite sensors and understand their limitations.
  • Make satellite-derived information more accessible to emergency responders, firefighters, land managers, and environmental researchers.
  • Support more informed wildfire monitoring and environmental decision-making.

The long-term vision is to contribute to more reliable multi-satellite fire monitoring and provide a foundation for expanding the analysis to additional regions and datasets. The platform is an analytical and monitoring aid, not a validated fire-spread prediction or operational early-warning system.

Tools and technologies

Our development combines scientific data processing with modern web technologies:

  • Data source: NASA FIRMS active fire datasets from MODIS and VIIRS.
  • Programming languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Frontend: React, HTML, CSS, and Javascript.
  • Backend: Python-based services and command-line tools.
  • Scientific computing: NumPy and Pandas for data processing and analysis.
  • Visualization: Interactive geographic maps, temporal charts, matplotlib charts, and analytical dashboards.
  • Development tools: Git, GitHub, and Visual Studio Code.

What makes the project creative?

The creative aspect of Ember Atlas is that it goes beyond simply displaying satellite hotspots. Instead, it focuses on harmonizing observations from two different satellite systems and communicating their differences through a unified interactive platform. It combines scientific data processing, geographic visualization, temporal analysis, and practical alert communication in one application.

Factors considered during development

Our team considered differences in satellite resolution, detection characteristics, observation frequency, geographic coverage, data quality, missing observations, and temporal consistency. We also considered usability, scalability, scientific transparency, and the risk of presenting uncertain observations as confirmed fire activity.

By addressing these factors, Ember Atlas aims to transform separate satellite observations into more understandable and useful information for wildfire monitoring and research.
